subject: sst
prompt_en: Compare Fundamental Rights and Fundamental Duties, with one example of each.
prompt_hi: Maulik Adhikaar aur Maulik Kartavya ki tulna karo, har ek ka ek example do.
answer: Rights are freedoms and protections guaranteed to people that courts can enforce (e.g. right to equality, freedom of speech, free education for children aged 6–14). Duties are responsibilities citizens are expected to follow (e.g. respect the Constitution, the national flag and anthem; protect the environment; promote harmony).

subject: sst
prompt_en: Which organ of government is doing each job? (a) Parliament passes a new road-safety law. (b) Traffic police make sure people wear helmets. (c) A court decides whether a fine was fair.
prompt_hi: Har kaam sarkaar ka kaunsa ang kar raha hai? (a) Sansad naya sadak-suraksha kaanoon paas karti hai. (b) Traffic police dhyaan rakhti hai ki log helmet pehnein. (c) Adaalat tay karti hai ki jurmaana sahi tha ya nahi.
answer: (a) Legislature (makes laws); (b) Executive (carries out laws); (c) Judiciary (interprets laws and settles disputes).

subject: sst
prompt_en: Choose one Preamble ideal (justice, liberty, equality or fraternity). Where do you see it — or not see it — in your school or neighbourhood, and what is one thing you could do about it?
prompt_hi: Prastaavana ka ek aadarsh chuno (nyaay, swatantrata, samata ya bandhutva). Use tum apne school ya mohalle mein kahan dekhte ho — ya kahan nahi dekhte — aur tum uske liye kya ek kaam kar sakte ho?
answer: A good answer picks one ideal, gives a concrete local example (e.g. equality: all children play in the same team regardless of background; fraternity: celebrating each other's festivals) or a gap, and suggests a realistic action.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Teach a friend what the Constitution is using the idea of rules for a cricket tournament, and then explain the Preamble in two sentences.
prompt_hi: Cricket tournament ke niyamon ka example le kar dost ko samjhao ki Samvidhan kya hai, phir Prastaavana ko do vaakyon mein samjhao.
answer: Key idea: like a tournament rulebook that every team and umpire must follow, the Constitution is the supreme rulebook for the government and citizens. The Preamble says the people of India give themselves this Constitution to make India a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic and to secure justice, liberty, equality and fraternity for all.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Why was it important that the Constituent Assembly included members from many regions and communities, including women?
prompt_hi: Yeh kyun zaroori tha ki Samvidhan Sabha mein alag-alag kshetron aur samudaayon ke log, aur mahilaayein bhi, shaamil hon?
answer: So that the Constitution would reflect the needs, views and rights of all of India's diverse people, not just one group; everyone would see it as theirs and its protections would cover everyone.

subject: sst
prompt_en: A weaver wants rice, the rice farmer wants shoes, and the cobbler wants cloth. Explain the problem and show how they could still barter.
prompt_hi: Bunkar ko chaawal chahiye, chaawal wale kisaan ko joote chahiye, aur mochi ko kapda chahiye. Mushkil samjhao aur batao ki phir bhi ve barter kaise kar sakte hain.
answer: No pair has a double coincidence of wants. They can still trade in a circle: the weaver gives cloth to the cobbler, the cobbler gives shoes to the farmer, and the farmer gives rice to the weaver — but this needs all three to meet and agree, which is hard.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Why would it be hard to buy a single egg if all you had to trade was a goat?
prompt_hi: Agar tumhare paas badle mein dene ke liye sirf ek bakri ho, toh ek anda khareedna mushkil kyun hoga?
answer: A goat is worth far more than an egg and cannot be divided into small parts without destroying it; barter also has no common measure to work out how many eggs equal a goat.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Put these forms of exchange in the order they appeared: paper notes, barter, UPI payments, punch-marked metal coins, cowrie shells and grain as money.
prompt_hi: Lenden ke in tareekon ko sahi kram mein lagao: kaagaz ke note, barter, UPI payment, aahat (punch-marked) dhaatu ke sikke, kaudi aur anaaj ko paise ki tarah use karna.
answer: Barter → cowrie shells and grain (commodity money) → punch-marked metal coins → paper notes → UPI payments.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Why did metal coins replace cattle and grain as money?
prompt_hi: Dhaatu ke sikkon ne paise ke roop mein gaay-bail aur anaaj ki jagah kyun le li?
answer: Coins are durable (do not rot or die), easy to carry, divisible into small values, all the same for a given value, and stamped by an authority so people can trust them.

subject: sst
prompt_en: A timeline shows: about 6th century BCE – punch-marked coins; 1935 – Reserve Bank of India set up; 2016 – UPI launched. Describe this in words and work out how many years passed between the RBI's start and UPI's launch.
prompt_hi: Ek timeline mein hai: lagbhag chhathi shatabdi BCE – aahat sikke; 1935 – Reserve Bank of India bana; 2016 – UPI shuru hua. Ise shabdon mein batao aur RBI ke shuru hone se UPI tak kitne saal hue, nikaalo.
answer: Coins have been used in India for about 2,500 years, starting with punch-marked coins; the RBI was set up in 1935 to manage the country's money; UPI came in 2016 — 81 years after the RBI began.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Name the three functions of money and give an everyday example of each.
prompt_hi: Paise ke 3 kaam batao aur har ek ka roz ki zindagi se ek example do.
answer: Medium of exchange (paying the sabziwala for vegetables); measure of value (comparing a ₹40 notebook with a ₹20 pen); store of value (saving pocket money in a piggy bank or bank account to use later).

subject: sst
prompt_en: Compare shopping at a village market with barter and with money: one problem barter causes that money solves, for each function of money.
prompt_hi: Gaon ke bazaar mein barter aur paise se khareedari ki tulna karo: paise ke har kaam ke liye ek aisi mushkil batao jo barter mein hoti hai aur paisa hal kar deta hai.
answer: Exchange: barter needs a double coincidence of wants, money is accepted by all. Measure: barter has no common unit to compare a pot with rice, money gives prices. Store: grain or fish spoil, money can be saved.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Why does a ₹100 note have value even though the paper is worth very little?
prompt_hi: Kaagaz ki keemat bahut kam hone ke bawajood ₹100 ke note ki keemat kyun hoti hai?
answer: Because people trust it: it is issued by the Reserve Bank of India and backed by the government, and the law makes it legal tender, so everyone accepts it in payment.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Predict: what would happen if anyone could print rupee notes at home?
prompt_hi: Socho: agar koi bhi ghar par rupaye ke note chhaap sakta, toh kya hota?
answer: There would be far too much money chasing the same goods, so prices would shoot up; people would stop trusting the rupee, shops might refuse notes, and trade would break down.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Find the mistake: "When I pay by UPI, my phone creates the money, so I can keep paying even if my bank account is empty."
prompt_hi: Galti pakdo: "Jab main UPI se pay karta hoon, mera phone paisa bana deta hai, isliye bank account khaali hone par bhi main pay karta reh sakta hoon."
answer: The phone does not create money. UPI only moves money from your bank account to the receiver's bank account; if your account has no money, the payment fails.

subject: sst
prompt_en: At your local vegetable seller, in how many different ways do people pay? Give two safety rules for paying by UPI.
prompt_hi: Tumhare mohalle ke sabziwale ke paas log kitne tareekon se paise dete hain? UPI se pay karne ke do safety niyam batao.
answer: Ways: cash (notes and coins), UPI by scanning a QR code, sometimes credit (udhaar) noted in a book. Safety rules: never share your UPI PIN or OTP with anyone; you never need a PIN to receive money; check the receiver's name before paying; ignore calls or links asking for details.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Teach a friend why money was invented: start from the problems of barter and end with the three functions of money.
prompt_hi: Dost ko samjhao ki paisa kyun banaya gaya: barter ki mushkilon se shuru karo aur paise ke 3 kaamon par khatam karo.
answer: Key idea: barter needs a double coincidence of wants, has no common measure, cannot divide big items and goods spoil; money solves these by being a medium of exchange, a measure of value and a store of value, and it works because people trust it.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Compare a weekly haat, a shopping mall and an online store: prices, variety, and costs for the seller.
prompt_hi: Haftewaar haat, shopping mall aur online store ki tulna karo: daam, vividhta, aur bechne wale ke kharche.
answer: Haat: usually low prices and bargaining, everyday goods, sellers have low costs (no permanent shop). Mall: higher prices, wide variety and brands, high rent, electricity and staff costs. Online: many choices and home delivery, prices vary, costs for warehouses and delivery, but no shop rent.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Why are vegetables often cheaper at a weekly haat than at a shop in a mall?
prompt_hi: Haftewaar haat mein sabziyaan mall ki dukaan se aksar sasti kyun hoti hain?
answer: Haat sellers have low costs: no permanent shop, little rent, electricity or staff; many sell what they grew or made themselves, so fewer middlemen; buyers can bargain.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Put the tomato's journey in order: you buy it from the sabziwala; a farmer grows it; a wholesaler buys it in bulk at the mandi; the sabziwala buys a crate from the wholesaler.
prompt_hi: Tamatar ke safar ko kram mein lagao: tum sabziwale se khareedte ho; kisaan ugaata hai; mandi mein thok vyapaari bulk mein khareedta hai; sabziwala thok vyapaari se ek crate khareedta hai.
answer: Farmer grows it → wholesaler buys in bulk at the mandi → sabziwala (retailer) buys a crate → you (consumer) buy it.

subject: sst
prompt_en: A farmer gets about ₹10 per kg for tomatoes, but you pay ₹40 per kg. Why is there such a gap?
prompt_hi: Kisaan ko tamatar ke lagbhag ₹10 kilo milte hain, par tum ₹40 kilo dete ho. Itna fark kyun?
answer: At each step costs are added: transport, loading, storage, commission at the mandi, wastage of spoiled tomatoes, the shop's rent and each trader's profit.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Heavy rain destroys many tomato fields. Predict what happens to tomato prices, and explain using supply and demand.
prompt_hi: Bhaari baarish se tamatar ke kai khet barbaad ho jaate hain. Socho tamatar ke daam ka kya hoga, aur supply-demand se samjhao.
answer: Prices rise: supply falls sharply while people still want about the same amount (demand stays), so buyers compete for fewer tomatoes.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Before Diwali, many families want diyas and sweets. Predict what happens to their prices before and after the festival.
prompt_hi: Diwali se pehle bahut parivaaron ko diye aur mithaiyaan chahiye hoti hain. Socho tyohaar se pehle aur baad mein inke daam ka kya hoga.
answer: Before Diwali demand rises, so prices tend to go up; after the festival demand falls, so prices tend to come down (shops may even offer discounts).

subject: sst
prompt_en: Find the mistake: "When lots of mangoes arrive in the market in May, mango prices go up because there are so many."
prompt_hi: Galti pakdo: "Mai mein jab bazaar mein bahut saare aam aate hain, toh aam ke daam badh jaate hain kyunki aam bahut zyada hain."
answer: When supply is very large, prices usually fall, not rise: sellers compete to sell lots of mangoes before they spoil.

subject: sst
prompt_en: What do these marks tell a consumer: ISI, AGMARK, FSSAI number?
prompt_hi: Yeh nishaan grahak ko kya batate hain: ISI, AGMARK, FSSAI number?
answer: ISI: an industrial product (like a helmet, cooker or electric item) meets Bureau of Indian Standards quality standards. AGMARK: an agricultural product (like spices, ghee, honey) meets grading standards. FSSAI number: packaged food is made by a licensed or registered food business.

subject: sst
prompt_en: A shop charges ₹25 for a water bottle with an MRP of ₹20, "for cooling". Is this allowed? What can you do?
prompt_hi: Ek dukaan ₹20 MRP wali paani ki bottle ke ₹25 maangti hai, "thanda karne ke". Kya yeh sahi hai? Tum kya kar sakte ho?
answer: No: MRP is the maximum retail price including all taxes, and a shop cannot charge more than it. You can politely refuse, ask for a bill, and complain through the consumer helpline or a consumer commission.

subject: sst
prompt_en: A flow diagram shows: farmer sells wheat at ₹20/kg → wholesaler sells at ₹26/kg → shop sells at ₹34/kg → you. Describe the diagram in words and work out how much is added at each step.
prompt_hi: Ek flow diagram mein hai: kisaan gehun ₹20/kg bechta hai → thok vyapaari ₹26/kg → dukaan ₹34/kg → tum. Diagram ko shabdon mein samjhao aur har step par kitna juda, nikaalo.
answer: The farmer sells wheat to a wholesaler at ₹20/kg; the wholesaler adds ₹6 and sells to a shop at ₹26/kg; the shop adds ₹8 and sells to the consumer at ₹34/kg. In total ₹14 per kg is added after the farm.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Map the markets your family uses: where do you buy vegetables, clothes and a phone or electronics? Why that place for each — price, trust, variety or convenience?
prompt_hi: Apne parivaar ke bazaaron ka naksha banao: sabzi, kapde aur phone ya electronics kahan se khareedte ho? Har ek ke liye wahi jagah kyun — daam, bharosa, vividhta ya suvidha?
answer: A good answer names a real market for each item and gives a fitting reason (e.g. vegetables from a haat or sabziwala for freshness and price; clothes from a local market or mall for variety; electronics online or from a trusted shop for price comparison and warranty).

subject: sst
prompt_en: Teach a friend how buyers and sellers together affect prices, using a festival or a season example.
prompt_hi: Dost ko samjhao ki khareedne wale aur bechne wale milkar daam par kaise asar daalte hain, kisi tyohaar ya mausam ka example le kar.
answer: Key idea: when many buyers want something (high demand) or there is little of it (low supply), prices rise — e.g. rakhis before Raksha Bandhan or tomatoes after floods; when there is plenty or few want it, prices fall — e.g. mangoes at the peak of the season.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Is an online shopping app a market? Explain.
prompt_hi: Kya online shopping app ek bazaar hai? Samjhao.
answer: Yes: a market is wherever buyers and sellers meet to exchange goods or services; online, they meet through an app or website instead of a physical place.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Put in order: the Green Revolution; farming begins at Mehrgarh; Kallanai built on the Kaveri; Harappan farmers grow cotton.
prompt_hi: Kram mein lagao: Hari Kranti (Green Revolution); Mehrgarh mein kheti shuru; Kaveri par Kallanai bana; Harappa ke kisaan kapaas ugaate hain.
answer: Mehrgarh (c. 7000 BCE) → Harappan cotton (c. 2600 BCE) → Kallanai (c. 2nd century CE) → Green Revolution (1960s).

subject: sst
prompt_en: What are kharif and rabi crops? Give the sowing time and two examples of each.
prompt_hi: Kharif aur rabi fasalein kya hain? Bone ka samay aur har ek ke do example batao.
answer: Kharif: sown with the monsoon (about June–July), harvested about September–October — e.g. rice, maize, cotton, bajra. Rabi: sown about October–December, harvested about March–April — e.g. wheat, mustard, gram.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Sort these crops into kharif, rabi or zaid: rice, wheat, mustard, cotton, gram, maize, watermelon.
prompt_hi: In fasalon ko kharif, rabi ya zaid mein baanto: chaawal, gehun, sarson, kapaas, chana, makka, tarbooz.
answer: Kharif: rice, cotton, maize. Rabi: wheat, mustard, gram. Zaid: watermelon.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Why is rice grown as a kharif crop and wheat as a rabi crop?
prompt_hi: Chaawal kharif fasal ke roop mein aur gehun rabi fasal ke roop mein kyun ugaaya jaata hai?
answer: Rice needs a lot of water and warm temperatures, which the monsoon provides; wheat grows best in cool weather with moderate water, which the winter season provides (often with irrigation).

subject: sst
prompt_en: The Kallanai on the Kaveri is nearly 2,000 years old and still used. What does it tell us about ancient farming in India?
prompt_hi: Kaveri par Kallanai lagbhag 2,000 saal purana hai aur aaj bhi istemaal hota hai. Isse puraane Bharat ki kheti ke baare mein kya pata chalta hai?
answer: Ancient farmers and rulers understood rivers and engineering well enough to divert water to fields for irrigation, and built structures strong enough to last nearly two thousand years; irrigation was an important part of farming long ago.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Compare flood (canal) irrigation with drip irrigation: how water reaches the plant, and water use.
prompt_hi: Baadh (nahar) wali sinchaai aur drip sinchaai ki tulna karo: paani paudhe tak kaise pahunchta hai, aur kitna paani lagta hai.
answer: Flood irrigation: water from a canal or well floods the whole field; simple but much water is lost to evaporation and runoff. Drip irrigation: pipes with small holes drip water right at each plant's roots; it uses much less water and suits dry regions, but costs more to set up.

subject: sst
prompt_en: What was the Green Revolution, and what did it achieve?
prompt_hi: Hari Kranti (Green Revolution) kya thi, aur isne kya haasil kiya?
answer: From the mid-1960s India used high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice, more irrigation, fertilisers and machines; grain production rose sharply, especially in Punjab and Haryana, and India became self-sufficient in food grains instead of depending on imports.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Predict: if farmers in an area keep pumping groundwater to grow rice every year, what will happen over 20 years?
prompt_hi: Socho: agar kisi ilaake ke kisaan har saal chaawal ugaane ke liye zameen ka paani pump karte rahein, toh 20 saal mein kya hoga?
answer: The water table will keep falling; wells and tube-wells must be dug deeper, pumping costs rise, some wells dry up, and in the future there may not be enough water for farming or drinking.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Find the mistake: "The more chemical fertiliser a farmer uses, the healthier the soil becomes forever."
prompt_hi: Galti dhoondho: "Kisaan jitna zyada chemical khaad daalega, mitti hamesha ke liye utni hi zyada swasth hogi."
answer: Overusing chemical fertilisers can harm soil over time — it can damage soil life and structure and pollute water; healthy soil needs balanced nutrients, organic matter (manure, compost) and crop rotation, guided by soil testing.

subject: sst
prompt_en: Why are millets like jowar, bajra and ragi being encouraged again?
prompt_hi: Jowar, bajra aur ragi jaise mote anaaj (millets) ko phir se badhava kyun diya ja raha hai?
answer: They need far less water than rice, grow in poor soils and hot, dry conditions, cope better with climate change, and are very nutritious (fibre, iron, calcium); 2023 was the International Year of Millets.
